articles.title: It’s more than just a hat
articles.summary: The CEO of 1047 Games, maker of Splitgate 2, has apologized for his controversial “Make FPS Great Again” hat.
articles.body: There’s a line in showbiz that goes, “There’s no such thing as bad publicity.” Ian Proulx, CEO of Splitgate 2 developer 1047 Games, has recently learned the hard way that’s not entirely true. Last week, during the Summer Game Fest keynote livestream, Proulx came out to promote his game wearing a black hat that read “Make FPS Great Again” — an obvious reference to Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again slogan. The Splitgate 2 community, journalists, and regular gamers seized on the hat (and not, you know, the game), immediately calling the statement gross and tone deaf. As questions from the Splitgate 2 community poured in, Proulx doubled down on social media, saying that he would not apologize and that the hat wasn’t a political statement and should be taken at face value. Today, however, he’s singing a different tune. He posted on X with the simple caption, “No excuses, I’m sorry,” accompanied by a nearly three-minute video explaining the decision to wear the hat and the intention behind it. “We needed something to grab attention, and the honest truth is, we tried to think of something, and this is what we came up with,” Proulx said. He acknowledged that he was aware the hat would be controversial. His apology was not for the hat itself, but the discussion surrounding the hat within the Splitgate 2 community. Proulx claimed he did not want the division he himself sowed. “The reason I’m sorry is because of what this has done to the community,” he said. He continued: “We knew there would be some level of controversy, but we really saw this as a meme that was kind of stating our truth.” As Proulx was making his statement, a few miles away in Los Angeles’ fashion district, where the Summer Game Fest Play Days campus resides, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) was conducting raids snatching up people just going about their lives, raids that led to clashes between people protecting their neighbors and defenders of a cruel regime. When I reported on the Trump-evoking slogan and the backlash to it, some commenters responded that “it’s just a hat.” But it is not just a hat. Aping a political statement that has been used to enact state violence isn’t “a meme,” it is a continuation of that violence. I think of the people in attendance at the show and those who work at the YouTube Theater who are immigrants or have immigrant family members. I think of the worker at the City Market Social House, the venue where SGF holds its Play Days event, who told me about the protocol they have in case ICE shows up: how people can hide in a room in the basement and hand out cards so they don’t have to speak to ICE and potentially implicate themselves. Proulx’s statement, no matter its form, isn’t just in bad taste. It is a stark reminder to those people that their lives and families are at risk. And saying “I’m sorry, it was just a meme” isn’t enough.

articles.title: The Duskbloods Preview: FromSoftware's Multiplayer Switch 2 Exclusive Is Special, Here's How It Plays
articles.summary: With tabletop rules and Souls-style gameplay, The Duskbloods, a Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive, is ambitious even for FromSoftware.
articles.body:
The Duskbloods might be FromSoftware’s most complex and interesting game yet. Miyazaki cites TTRPG influences for its gameplay systems and multiplayer mechanics.

As far as gameplay feel, it's comparable to Bloodborne or Nightreign with added mobility and fit into an eight-player phase-based PvPvE setting where you earn victory points to avoid elimination.

The lock-on targeting and camera can have trouble tracking fast moving opponents, but the combat is intricate and intense.

FromSoftware isn't new to multiplayer. Invasions have been a staple in the Souls games and we just came off of Elden Ring's co-op twist with Nightreign. But The Duskbloods is something very different and new territory for the team, and to simply label it as a PvPvE game is to woefully undersell what it is. It has that familiar tough action combat packaged in phase-based matches where eight players compete for what are essentially victory points on a map in order to advance to subsequent phases, which then concludes in a three-player PvP brawl. I got to play about eight hours of The Duskbloods on a visit to FromSoftware in Tokyo, and while there are a ton of nuances I'll dissect in this preview, I'll say upfront that it has the makings of another hit in the Souls lineage where fun is found in the challenge and the mysteries of its world propel you to keep pushing – just now in the context of a competitive multiplayer Switch 2 exclusive. If any team can pull off such a wild idea, it'd be director Hidetaka Miyazaki and company. So buckle up y'all, The Duskbloods just might be the most complex and most fascinating project to come out of FromSoftware yet.

The build I played alongside other media and content creators is the same as the network test, and all the gameplay you're seeing here was provided by Nintendo and FromSoftware since we were not permitted to record our own. You'll notice the UI is removed and that there are specific features I'm not able to show, so I'll need to lay some groundwork since The Duskbloods has a lot of moving parts.

This is a multiplayer-only Switch 2 game, and eight players queue into a match as one of several characters known as the Bloodsworn, each of which have their own weapons, ranged attacks, and special abilities. Every match has three phases that last about eight minutes each where you must earn Virtue points to survive The Culling – and while everyone always makes it past Phase I, the bottom two players are eliminated after Phase II and the bottom three are gone after Phase III. That leaves three players who are transported to a closed-off combat arena under a blood-red sky to duke it out in the finale called the Moon Blood Bestowal. A full match can last about 30 minutes, but when all four parts are varied and feel like an intense race against the clock and other players, it's easy to lock in and stay focused as every moment counts.

Now, how do you earn Virtue points? There are Commendations that award points to the players with the most PvE enemy kills (called Bloodfang Virtue ) and/or the most items collected (called Collector Virtue ) – this can change as the match goes on since points will be awarded and taken away based on how you stack against others, but these stats are never displayed. There is also Flame Virtue , which are collectible purple embers on the thrones of skeletons found in specific regions of the map – the region where these spawn is randomized in each phase, but their locations within that region seem to be similar. Repulsion Virtue is given when killing powerful computer-controlled enemies called Trespassers that are marked on the map – they vary in difficulty, and they can take a long time to defeat and may not be the best use of time early in a match. Each Bloodsworn also has what's called a Sigil , which is a unique objective for that character and completing it rewards Virtue points (but more on that later).

Lastly, my favorite method of earning Virtue is through what are called Rituals , because this is where things get really spicy between players. In the back-half or so of Phases II and III, a certain section of the map will be outlined in gold, signifying the Ritual Site with four or five capture points marked within that boundary, turning the match into a King-of-the-Hill-style game. Capturing a point rewards you with Pledge Virtue , however, you have to hold the action button for about 10 seconds to capture it, thus leaving you vulnerable to other players and enemies who might be barreling down on you. Furthermore, other players can steal your capture point which then takes away your Virtue and gives it to them. I love swooping in to capture a point right when they open and hoping no one else contests it, but the tension goes crazy when I have to hold onto and defend my point. And this is where the PvP component really matters – only within Ritual Sites can you earn Sword Virtue, which rewards you for killing other players. It truly turns into a PvP zone when you're trying to capture points, defend them, and fight other players, but the Virtue you gain can stack quickly and shoot you up the rankings.

The element of surprise works wonders, since getting the jump on players by using your map knowledge and your Bloodsworn's abilities effectively will make quick work of them. And the push-and-pull dynamic this creates is absolutely thrilling. It's worth noting that you'll keep respawning in matches so dying doesn't mean elimination, and you're not obligated to participate in Rituals since it's more like a map event, but it's high-risk / high-reward, and for the sickest of Souls sickos like me, the risk is oh-so compelling. If you decide to take part, you'll want to look out for Goldstones and Redstones , which are items that spawn around the Ritual Site; these will boost the Virtue gained from capturing points or killing other players, respectively.

Phases II and III may also get randomized map events to shake things up. One I kept getting allowed me to call in airstrikes from a zeppelin that lingers up in the sky, which can decimate anything within range, including yourself – definitely handy for keeping folks away from my precious Ritual spots. But some are opportunities to earn more Virtue, like one that rewards the first player to ring the bell atop the tallest building on the map. I was able to do this before anyone else by finding clever ways of climbing up the tower, and it was chaos having five others scrambling on the way up and taking potshots at each other.

I was able to consistently make it to the finale since I grasped the Virtue system quickly. But the three-player PvP brawl here at the end taps into a whole different skillset, and almost had us moving like it was a fighting game or one of those 3D arena brawlers. It can be overwhelming if you don't know how to manage the chaos. There isn't as much room for trickery in the closed arena, so it's more about reading your opponents and really understanding what their specific Bloodsworn is capable of while keeping your head on a swivel, especially when everyone has a summoned NPC companion to fight alongside them. Each player has two lives so there are opportunities to make a comeback, but if you can't hang with the speed and demand of head-to-head PvP, it can be rough going. That's the Souls-style challenge, but damn is it rewarding when you pull it off in the end.

Let me take a step back for a moment because there's a lot more that goes into pursuing Virtue points and getting combat-ready. You have to level-up in-match to get stronger, gain more HP and stamina, and build out your Bloodsworn's capabilities. If you're not defeating enemies at a solid pace, you can end up underpowered later in the match, so it's important to stay active every second. You can gain EXP fairly quickly and end up around level 17 or 20 by the final phase, but you gotta be grinding.

Each Bloodsworn gains a new special ability at level 12 as well, and these are so important to have in tough battles. For example, my favorite Bloodsworn Trang Lanh has a cloaking ability to start, but at level 12 she can then summon a massive snake to direct heavy AoE damage and knockback. Meanwhile, the noble skeleton Senator Samir Patres can transform into a dinosaur that homes in on targets, chews them up, and tosses them aside, which became an early favorite during the preview.

We had access to six Bloodsworn (10 are planned for the full release), and they were all distinct enough to form a unique approach. Sniper Layla has melee attacks of course, but she emphasizes long-range shots as her name would imply and almost plays like it's a third-person shooter. Albert is your sort of all-rounder, while the pajama boy Bloodhand Jan sports an axe and mage-like fire spells. However, I can't tell you how many times the armor-clad chicken man named Zork knocked me on my ass with his jetpack rushdown (yeah, I'm beefing with my roommate Blessing Adeoye Jr. from Kinda Funny who was maining Zork at this preview). But that's part of learning how to play The Duskbloods, it's about understanding movesets and knowing how to counter what you're up against when it comes time for PvP.

Furthermore, these characters have their own Sigils you can activate before a match. As I mentioned earlier, these are objectives unique to them – for example, Trang Lanh's Sigil makes you seek out a certain player as a target and the Senator lets you propose to another player in hopes they'll accept. This is one area that director Hidetaka Miyazaki told me he's paying attention to with regards to player reception as these are one of the wild cards that can affect the typical cadence of a match.

As far as gameplay feel, it's comparable to Bloodborne or Nightreign, not quite Sekiro in terms of speed. You have a block, a parry with a perfect-timed block, and a sonic howl that will stagger enemies when executed in the parry window. You can then bite the neck of staggered enemies which causes big damage and heals you, and when done to weaker enemies, will turn them into minions who follow you around the map to fight for you.

More importantly, NPC companions called Kin are one of the biggest keys to success in The Duskbloods. You'll find glowing symbols across the map to summon Kin who will accompany you for the rest of the match – depending on their type, they can either fight alongside you or provide support. They level up independently and are another way to create "a build" of sorts throughout the match. If they die, they'll go on cooldown before being able to return to the field.

While there will be three maps at launch, we only got to play one map called Lowanro City, and it evokes a bit of the grim Victorian vibe of Bloodborne, especially as it gets deeper into the night with each passing phase. At the start of a phase, you choose the general area to spawn into and you'll get a random spot within it. Foggy swamps, a towering cathedral, dirty city streets, crowded rooftops, poisonous sewers, and a bridge that runs through the middle of the map – these all make up the interconnected regions. Markers on the map indicate which regions have which perks during the phase, such as Flame Virtue, weapons perks, or bonus Kin EXP, for example. And getting to and from these hotspots efficiently is such an important key to success. Even after about eight hours of gametime, I was still discovering the intricacies of the map and formulating new tactics just as I thought it was starting to get repetitive – if the first one is this dense, I'm hyped to see what the others can offer.

Verticality is very much a highlight in The Duskbloods, too. No, you don't get a double jump, or a triple jump, but a quadruple jump and an airdash along with it, and you can charge up the first jump to fly into the air. Along with infinite sprint, this movement system makes things feel fast-paced and match the hustle required once the clock starts ticking. Hopping across rooftops, boosting up to floors above, and, well, airdashing isn't what you'd typically expect in a Souls-style game, but it works well for navigating such a varied map quickly. Part of me wants to say this plays closer to a character-action game like Devil May Cry at times, especially when PvP battles start to break out.

This brings me to my main complaint with The Duskbloods – the lock-on targeting system. Souls games haven't always been great about camera angles and targeting, and those issues are exacerbated with the speed of this game and with the frenetic movement of actual human players. The camera whips at breakneck speed when a targeted player charge-jumps into the air, and it sometimes just doesn't read certain enemies in the field when trying to swap targets. It's sort of an impossible task with this particular style of action game, but I hope there will be improvements with smarter camera behavior or just on-screen readability when multiple players and their Kin are flying all over the place. One tactic I began using was to just try keeping everything in front me to mitigate the limitations of the camera and lock-on system.

Perhaps the co-op DNA can take some of the edge off, too. When facing Trespassers, you can temporarily link up with other players to split the work and all participants get Virtue points if the group defeats. You can also queue into duos matches where two players share Virtue points to advance – the difference being that in the final phase, it's the two best teams who go into a 2v2 fight for victory. So, The Duskbloods doesn't always have to be a lonely endeavor.

Miyazaki said it himself that board games and tabletop RPGs were a definite influence when coming up with the rules and mechanics for The Duskbloods. Thankfully, there's a lengthy tutorial that does just enough to prepare you – he admits that it is the most complex game he's worked on, but like a good board game, once you grasp the rules and get enough reps, matches will start to flow naturally.

This was just the Network Test, meaning it's a small portion of what will be available on launch. FromSoftware doesn't have a release date or even a release window yet, and it seemed like Miyazaki and the team are still working out the game's features while looking at the Network Test as a way to finally get player feedback for adjustment. In our conversation, he emphasized character customization and different options that can change the way you approach matches if you don't exactly love the PvP aspect so you can still work toward unlocking additional features for characters and story content back at the hub area called The House of Night. These things aren't in place quite yet.

I asked him if he's concerned about a skill gap growing as time goes on, given the emphasis on PvP. Miyazaki said matchmaking will account for skill level, but the team is also working on systems to incentivize veteran players to assist newcomers and for ways to make the early game feel more welcoming. He said story cutscenes and progression won't be so reliant on winning matches either, so making it to the final phase and focusing more on the PvE aspects will still be rewarding. However, if you are a PvP fiend, he hinted at an Invasion-style option where you can be a ninth player dropping into an ongoing match to simply fight other players, and perhaps that'll be another one of those curveballs FromSoft likes throwing into its games.

I really enjoyed what I played because The Duskbloods is clearly built for those who crave discovery, enjoy the unexpected nature of FromSoft's work, and the sort of meta you'd see in fighting games. It'll be a tricky balancing act with all these moving parts while trying to maintain an audience for a fairly complex game on Switch 2. Miyazaki didn't seem too concerned, though, saying that even though he's not great at action games himself, he wanted to build something that he would enjoy, and I suppose that's all you can do in a time when multiplayer games struggle to find their footing. FromSoft has the chops, and I can't wait to see what The Duskbloods becomes when it actually comes out.

While you're here, check out these previews of other big upcoming games we've played recently!

Michael Higham is an editor at IGN who regularly contributes with reviews, previews, features, and news in written and video form. He's usually entrusted with covering long RPGs and tech products, but he's got range when it comes to games. You'll also catch him at events and hosting video content, including IGN's weekly podcast Unlocked .

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 Will Have RPG Mechanics Like Eating, Exercising, and More
articles.summary: Some of the first gameplay details for Grand Theft Auto 6 have been confirmed, and it seems like Rockstar is embracing a more RPG-y style this time around.
articles.body:
Some of the first gameplay details for Grand Theft Auto 6 have been confirmed, and it seems like Rockstar is embracing a more RPG-type style this time around.

As part of a cover story for Dazed magazine , Rockstar Games revealed heaps of new information about Grand Theft Auto 6. Arguably the most notable details revolve around some of its gameplay features. In GTA 6, players will be able to eat, work out, and sleep, all of which have an impact on the game's two protagonists, Jason and Lucia. Players will have to take care of the Bonnie and Clyde-esque couple, as eating will affect their weight, working out will visibly change their build and strength, and a lack of sleep will negatively impact their features. It's unclear if a lack of sleep will impact the actual gameplay, or if they'll just look sleep-deprived, but it's a clear sign of Rockstar's attention to detail.

For many, this may remind them of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. That game featured a lot of RPG mechanics that allowed CJ to fluctuate in weight and fitness. Later games largely dropped these elements, but GTA 5 featured a stat system that allowed players to enhance their stamina and strength by doing physical activities such as running, playing sports, and riding bikes.

Additionally, there is also a social media feed for players to scroll, something fans have speculated about since the game's reveal in 2023. Character switching is also returning from GTA 5, allowing players to play as a couple or split up and operate independently. Dazed teased that the relationship between these two is a major focus of the game and that choices made by the player have "repercussions that cut much deeper" than the honor system in the Red Dead Redemption series.

“We look back at our previous games with a critical eye and see where we want to evolve based on what we didn’t do as well as we would have liked to, either because we didn’t have the time, resources or technological capabilities, or in some cases things we just didn’t do as well or consider as fully as we could have,” said Rob Nelson, co-studio head at Rockstar North. “A lot of what we do is very iterative — we adjust a lot of things by feel based on what is working and what isn’t.”

Based on that information, it's possible that there will be some kind of relationship meter that can impact how Jason and Lucia feel about each other. Ultimately, it sounds like Rockstar is making a much more nuanced and interactive game. That should hardly come as a surprise following Red Dead Redemption 2, but it seems like Rockstar is really pushing the envelope with GTA 6. Tomorrow, fans will get a proper look at the game thanks to an extended look releasing on Netflix at 3 PM ET , with a YouTube version to follow six hours later.

GTA 6 has suffered from a plethora of leaks over the last week, including a story-focused one earlier today . Rockstar Games released a statement this morning confirming that the situation was "heartbreaking," but it is working hard to deliver a product that exceeds expectations.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will release on November 19th for Xbox Series X|S and PS5.

articles.title: The Frosthaven Board Game Gets a Rare Discount on Amazon
articles.body:
Update : This deal is now 100% claimed and no longer available.

Frosthaven is one of the best board games on the market. It served as a follow up to the immensely popular Gloomhaven board game, and is one of the most imposing dungeon-delving board games you can buy. It's also really quite expensive.

It's not often that we see any sort of discount on this game, but Amazon currently has a Lightning Deal running that drops it down to its lowest price ever. For a limited time (or while stock lasts), you can pick up this massive board game for $153. The discount is set to expire around 7:45pm PT or when the deal is fully claimed.

Frosthaven comes as an enormous box full of stuff. There's an incredibly thick rulebook, decks of cards, trays, dividers, a map, and miniatures. All-in-all, there are a few hundred hours worth of gameplay that comes packaged in a rather large box. And if you already own Gloomhaven characters and items, you can use them in this game as well. It's a massive campaign game that can be pretty daunting for casual players.

articles.title: Fans Mourn Tim Curry After Legendary Actor Dies at 80 Years Old
articles.summary: Prolific British actor Tim Curry has died aged 80, leaving behind a storied legacy that includes iconic roles in productions like The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Muppet Treasure Island, Home Alone 2, and many more.
articles.body:
Prolific British actor Tim Curry has died aged 80, leaving behind a storied legacy that includes iconic roles in productions like The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Muppet Treasure Island, Home Alone 2, and many more.

News of Curry’s death was announced on August 26, 2026 by his long-term manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz, who confirmed the star died at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles.

Curry suffered a severe stroke in 2012 that left him wheelchair bound, causing lasting issues in his left leg. The actor opened up about the incident in an interview with CBS in October 2025, revealing that the stroke had even impacted his ability to speak.

“I had to learn how to speak again,” he explained. “That was very weird. I hated not being able to speak because I speak a lot. I have to be told to shut up a lot. I love words, I love to communicate.”

Despite his physical limitations as a result of the stroke, Curry continued to work, notably returning to Rocky Horror for the 2016 televised remake of the musical as the story’s narrator, The Criminologist.

Curry was born on April 19, 1946 in Grappenhall, Cheshire. He graduated from the University of Birmingham with a BA in English and drama in 1968. That same year, he joined the original cast of the musical Hair in London, a project that would lead him to meet actor and playwright Richard O’Brien, who famously penned his role as Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show.

Curry’s performance in the musical, which came to film in 1975, skyrocketed the actor to fame, kicking off the heyday of his career in the 90s and 2000s. Millennials will remember him best as the cagey hotel concierge from Home Alone 2: Lost in New York , Long John Silver in Muppet Treasure Island , and Pennywise the Clown in the 1990 miniseries adaptation of Steven King’s IT .

Curry also boasted a swath of famous voice acting roles, having lent his talents to animated films like FernGully: The Last Rainforest , The Wild Thornberries Movie, and the English dub of Studio Ghibli’s The Cat Returns.

Curry’s last major role in a live-action film was playing Alexander Monro in the 2010 British comedy Burke & Hare. He notably made an appearance at a September 2025 screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show for the film’s 50th anniversary, where he shared more details about his stroke.

“I was having a massage at the time and I didn’t even actually notice anything, but the guy who was doing the massage said, ‘I’m worried about you, I want to call an ambulance.’ And he did, and I said, ‘That’s so silly.’ I still can’t walk, which is why I’m in this silly chair, and that’s very limiting. So I won’t be singing and I won’t be dancing very soon. I still have real problems with my left leg,” the actor shared.

As noted by The Hollywood Reporter , Curry answered that he wasn’t afraid of dying in response to a question during his October 2025 interview with CBS. “No, I’m not. I don’t fear death. I try to avoid it, as I think we all do, but I suspect that in the end I will welcome it,” he said.

The entertainment world is mourning the loss of two legends in just as many days, with country music legend Dolly Parton's death being announced by her nephew yesterday, August 25.

articles.title: Game of Thrones: War for Westeros – The First Hands-On Preview
articles.summary: Game of Thrones: War of Westeros is shaping up to be an impressive RTS, especially for folks that are looking to scratch that base-building fantasy itch. Still, from the other three launch factions, to the campaign mode, to even how larger matches will play out, all remain as much of a mystery as the release date for Winds of Winter. But for fans that have been hungry for some base-building, PlaySide looks poised to deliver quite the feast.
articles.body:
I only got to try the 1v1 Skirmish mode on two different maps.

Visually, War for Westeros adopts the look and feel from the show, with heroes like Jon Snow and Tywin Lannister both looking like their respective actors.

The camera was problematic in my preview build.

Having grown up in the ‘90s, an era when base-building RTS games were far more prevalent than they are today, I have a special fondness for this variety of strategy game. So when a new one gets announced nowadays, the wave of nostalgia washes over me, and I take notice. That’s exactly what happened when PlaySide announced the upcoming Game of Thrones: War for Westeros RTS back at Summer Game Fest 2025. Recently, I had a chance to ride into battle waving the banner of House Stark and Lannister in an early build of the game, coming away knowing a bit more now than Jon Snow.

Set in the era of the mainline series of A Song of Ice and Fire as opposed to the prequels of House of the Dragon or A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, War for Westeros has players hoist the banners and take command of some of their favorite Great Houses. These include the likes of the Starks from the North, the lions of the Lannisters, Daenerys Targaryen and her dragons, or even the frozen hordes of the Whitewalkers themselves. The build that I had a chance to check out was a bit less grand, consisting of 1v1 online and offline skirmish modes with the choices of fielding the armies of either Stark or Lannister, with two smallish maps to pick from.

Visually, War for Westeros adopts the look and feel from the show, with heroes like Jon Snow and Tywin Lannister both looking like their respective actors — Kit Harington and Charles Dance — and drops them onto an already impressive-looking battlefield. Even in this Alpha state, I was impressed with just how good War for Westeros is looking. Watching flaming arrows rain down on Lannister structures and set them on fire as they crumble, or the brilliant emerald flames of Wildfire engulfing poor Robb Stark as the pyromancers hurl their precarious projectiles, were always delights to watch.

The rest of the game, outside of the death and destruction, is already looking pretty damn good too, and even though only two of the factions were playable, I got the sense that PlaySide is putting great care into making sure the aesthetics of the various houses look distinct. You could zoom in and see the Stark units, adorned with fur capes and the armor that living in the north would require, their structures built from sturdy lumber and grey stone, while the Lannisters fielded soldiers in gold-and-crimson armor, their buildings draped with the lion’s banner.

The distinction between Stark and Lannister is far deeper than simply “one side has wolves and the other lions” (just to be clear, the Lannisters don’t have lion units as far as I know). Both armies can unleash all sorts of unique units with varying abilities and strengths, which I eagerly took advantage of, with both armies requiring their own strategy and build order to take advantage of.

Starting off first with House Stark, these northerners are powerhouses, with some fantastic cavalry options to run straight through the lines of much of what the Lannisters can put out there. In a bit of a surprising twist, the Stark faction is able to recruit and train not only powerful Night’s Watch Brothers, with both melee and ranged options to pick from, but also Wildlings and some of the beasts that call the realm beyond the walls home.

Helping to lead the north’s forces, the likes of Robb Stark, Jon Snow, and their respective dire wolves served as the faction’s hero units. These special hero units will level up as they take out enemy forces, learning more and more powerful abilities as they go, at the expense of longer recruit times and higher cost to do so, should they unfortunately fall in battle. Jon Snow, for instance, will inspire those around him, making his nearby troops deal more damage and imparting some damage resistance while having another ability that lets him deliver a savaging sword strike and causing a bleed effect.

“Lannisters always repay their debts,” and that is thanks largely to them being stinkin' rich, a fact that PlaySide has used to help define the faction. The Lannisters’ gold production structures produce more of the given resource per structure, granting them a faster rate of getting gold and can make their builders work faster by lining their pockets with a bit of extra coin. Coupled with the ability at any time to turn their gold into influence, and vice versa - influence being the other resources used for building and training your more advanced structures and units- this house had a vastly easier and faster early game compared to the folks from the North. While the Starks gain all their allies through more traditional training methods, the Lannisters can purchase contracts for a variety of mercenary companies to hire their fighters, each with different strengths.

Jaime and Tywin serve as the Lannisters’ heroes, with the younger of the lions serving best on the front lines, while Tywin leads from atop his horse. Tywin can negate debuffs on his troops while strengthening his own cavalry. Jaime, being a master swordsman, can deliver some devastating strikes on single targets while also taunting enemies to target him instead. Alternatively, using his menacing history as a Kingslayer can slow and damage enemies near him over time.

Right out of the gate, sides will only have access to a small plot of land, where they can start expanding and building out their bases. You have your seat of power, your home base you have to protect from being destroyed (thus losing you the game), but then you will also need to expand your reach by constructing barracks, archery rangers, and resource-generating buildings. Some of these are locked until others have been constructed first. Anyone who grew up with the likes of StarCraft, Command and Conquer, or more recently the Age of Empires series with their remakes will have the general gist of how Westeros plays out.

To expand your workable land, War for Westeros breaks the overall map into captureable regions, with a tower that can be held to allow your workers to start building in that region. In the small 1v1-tailored battlefields that I had access to, these regions would also feature resource-rich points that can allow you to build advanced versions of your production buildings like the Lannisters' Mine Shafts or Stark's Windmills, which allow you to really bump up your production line. A few of these regions’ spaces, though, had something I found to be even cooler, and in some respects, that I found to be more impactful and important to getting that W – camps.

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros Screenshots

These camps spawn neutral hostile mobs that you can kill and will net you some gold as a reward. Rushing to get a squad of soldiers built and sent out to kill these mobs quickly became my go-to strategy during the early game. Its injection of resources saved my butt more than once by allowing me to quickly start training another unit to protect my new expansion into the region or allow me to start constructing the next building in my tree. And the fact that they would respawn every couple of minutes meant I could park some knights and archers nearby and use them as another source of income. It’s a trick that I used in another similar sort of game years ago, and one I hadn't thought of much until now.

With each match I played, War for Westeros kept reminding me of another amazing RTS game based on an epic fantasy book series: The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth 2. (Side note: It is, depressingly, a game that is unavailable digitally anywhere, at least officially.) From how heroes behave to the more spread-out building placement and of course the random mobs you would want to kill, playing War for Westeros takes me back to leading the forces of Gondor against my friend and his annoying army of Dwarves.

Even in this small snippet, War for Westeros is already presenting itself as an RTS that can be fun regardless of whether you consider yourself a seasoned battlefield general or just someone wanting to get vengeance for Ned Stark by slaughtering a whole host of Lions. Against easier CPU adversaries in earlier games, I would just click and train whatever units looked cool just to see what the armies were all about and did just fine, but the more time I spent and the harder the foes got, using the hotkeys to assign orders to specific groups, playing to a unit’s strength to counter specific enemies, and knowing when best to use my heroes’ abilities became critical to avoid getting crushed. And this was only with two of the factions; I can't wait to see how the wild clashes and strategies will evolve once the rest of the armies are introduced.

But, as a game still in development, there are certainly some areas that I hope get tweaked or adjusted prior to the final release. Tooltips are a bit sparse, such as giving you specifics on what the bonuses are when you garrison a worker inside a building, and the marker showing what direction your units will face is pretty tiny and easily obscured by details on the map, like trees and grass. Perhaps my bigger request, however, is with the camera. Buildings are big, armies can get equally imposing, and I frequently would find myself scrolling my mouse wheel down in a futile attempt to pull back my view even farther. Give me a high-up, bird's-eye- or in this case, a Three-eyed Raven’s eye view, of the battlefield, and let me see the whole of these epic clashes.

Game of Thrones: War of Westeros is shaping up to be an impressive RTS, especially for folks that are looking to scratch that base-building fantasy itch. Still, from the other three launch factions, to the campaign mode, to even how larger matches will play out, all remain as much of a mystery as the release date for Winds of Winter. But for fans that have been hungry for some base-building, PlaySide looks poised to deliver quite the feast.

While you're here, check out these previews of other big upcoming games we've played recently!

articles.title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation Gets Pending Mature 17+ Rating, and Fan Theories Are Already Going Wild
articles.summary: Final Fantasy VII Revelation is available to wishlist on all major platforms, and fans have noticed that its pending rating is a bit more intense than they expected.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation is available to wishlist on all major platforms, and fans have noticed that its pending rating on the Xbox store is a bit more intense than they expected.

Set to release in Spring 2027, the last entry in the Final Fantasy VII Remake Trilogy wraps up the saga for Cloud and company in their quest to protect the planet from the incoming Meteor.

We’ve gotten a few glimpses at gameplay over the last few months, showing off submarine combat, traversal via the Highwind, and an explanation of the new FITS system — but none of these point to a Mature rating.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

That’s the current predicted rating that’s listed on the game’s Xbox page , which says, “Rating pending, likely Mature 17+.” As clarified by the ESRB’s rating system , the Mature rating is given to games that may contain “intense violence, blood and gore, sexual content and/or strong language.”

For now, the game’s rating is still pending, and the Mature prediction is simply a placeholder implemented by the ESRB likely based on many publicly unknown factors prior to its official rating. But why would Revelation be rated Mature, when the first two games in the trilogy were rated T for Teen?

There’s a couple possible explanations for this. The first could be that the ESRB is using the placeholder out of an abundance of caution due to Final Fantasy XVI , which was notably rated Mature due to its sexual themes, language, and overall violence.

The other explanation is that there could be a lot more violence, language, and sexual themes in this particular game… and that possibility is sending fans into a tizzy.

Most can’t help but bring up that saucy scene between Clive and Jill in FF16, wondering if the famous "Highwind scene" between Cloud and Tifa might get a bit more heated than was originally portrayed in the 1997 game.

“I BEG YOUR FINEST PARDON?” one fan wrote on X. “Mature 17+?! Spicy Highwind scene confirmed??? Hello?!”

articles.title: The Duskbloods Feels Like a Nintendo Party Game in a Bloody Wrapper
articles.summary: Once you go beneath the surface of its wonderfully grotesque, unwelcoming exterior that’s right in line with FromSoftware’s house style, The Duskbloods plays so much like a classic multiplayer Nintendo game.
articles.body:
If you’d told me two years ago that Nintendo and FromSoftware would team up on an online PvPvE Switch 2 exclusive that’s also kind of a spiritual successor to Bloodborne, my first reaction would have been, “it’s called the Switch 2??” But jokes aside, I would’ve found this collaboration hard to believe.

FromSoftware is one of the hottest devs on the planet right now, but its games rarely come to Nintendo platforms. Nintendo is publishing this game outside of Japan, and you can count all of the M-rated games the typically family-friendly company has ever published on basically two hands. Both companies also have long histories of fairly clunky online multiplayer, making the type of game they’ve gone in on together stand out even more. On paper, it’s a bizarre partnership, but after spending around eight hours with The Duskbloods network test last weekend, I totally get it now.

In IGN’s interview with FromSoftware’s Hidetaka Miyazaki , he spoke about how the deal came to be, stating that Nintendo was “very excited and receptive” to the idea from the jump. And now that I’ve played it, it’s so easy to see why folks at Nintendo thought this would be a good fit for Switch, because once you go beneath the surface of its wonderfully grotesque, unwelcoming exterior that’s right in line with FromSoftware’s house style, The Duskbloods plays so much like a classic multiplayer Nintendo game.

Before I jumped into the network test, a coworker pointed out that The Duskbloods is basically Bloodborne mixed with Kirby Air Ride’s City Trial (or Super Smash Bros. for 3DS’ Smash Run), and I can’t unsee that comparison. A bunch of players drop into a large map and have a limited amount of time to level up, find new powers, and contend with random field events, all in preparation for a final round where one player is crowned the victor.

It’s stuffed with crazy powerups and last-second comebacks, and it all revolves around a core belief that you don’t have to be the best, or even win, to still have a great time. That philosophy has fueled the best Nintendo party games like Mario Kart and Super Smash Bros. for decades, and The Duskbloods takes those concepts and brilliantly packages them in a very different, bloodstained wrapper. I only claimed victory in a single match over the whole weekend, but every time I lost the final bout or was culled before I got there, I excitedly queued right up to try again.

My favorite moment happened because of a random item I found that completely turned the tide in my favor. I don’t remember its exact name – and screenshots and video capture were disabled for the Network Test so I can’t really check – but it was essentially a pocket watch that let me add 30 seconds to the phase’s countdown timer. Nobody knew I had this power, and it was up to me to use its shock factor to the greatest effect.

I waited patiently to strike, perched high above a stake I wished to claim as my own to earn enough Virtue Points to advance to the next phase. Its current holder was defending the perimeter, but with about 10 seconds to go, they left to rack up some last-second kills. 10 seconds isn’t really enough time for someone to show up and steal those precious points, right? But 40 seconds is. I turned back time, leapt down, and stole the virtue for myself, just barely earning enough to move onto my first-ever finale. I promptly got crushed, but I didn’t care. That brief moment of triumph is what I’ll carry with me.

Despite loving Elden Ring and Nightreign, FromSoftware PvP has never been my strong suit. I play all sorts of other competitive multiplayer games, but something about FromSoftware’s methodical combat has never entirely clicked with me. So, I didn’t really expect to like The Duskbloods all that much. But apparently, Miyazaki designed The Duskbloods with a similar perspective in mind: “Personally, I am not very great at these high-intensity action games and things like PvP,” Miyazaki said. “So, at the start, the audience really is just myself while thinking about how I would go at this. Are there systems in place that I would enjoy, that cater to me as a player, not being someone who's really into that intense PvP? That's a lot of where it starts.”

Dying isn’t an enormous setback. Instead, it represents opportunity cost, burning valuable seconds you could be spending getting better, so you’re still motivated to stay alive as much as possible. But I found myself less hesitant to challenge a boss I might be underleveled for, and the whole map began to feel like my gothic playground.

Its unique ruleset also deemphasizes PvP outside of specific scenarios and zones. I was worried that I’d just be killed on sight any time I ran into another player, but getting into skirmishes outside of limited-time areas that explicitly reward you for killing others is rarely your best move.

That’s not to say there wasn’t some combination of trolls and players that just didn’t understand the objective that would kill me for seemingly no reason, and there are occasionally side objectives that do pit players against each other in unusual circumstances, but for the most part, I felt like I was left on my own to prepare for the Ritual Site’s opening. It’s in these stretches that The Duskbloods’ board game inspirations are most legible. In board games, you’re often indirectly competing with opponents for resources and victory points, only coming directly at odds with each other at certain moments, and The Duskbloods nails that dynamic.

When everyone does come together, it’s fantastic chaos. There’s a Smash Bros.-like nature in strategically waiting to strike while more powerful players duke it out, swooping in at the last second to steal the kill. The best player doesn’t always win, and if you bring in the right summon, items, and strategy, you can hold your own. There’s also a built-in rubber-banding mechanic to keep things close: Players on the bottom of the Virtue Point ladder get an attack boost when fighting someone above them.

After the clock hits zero at the end of each phase, there are a few seconds where all of my remaining competitors kind of just walk around and look at each other before the screen fades to black. It feels like the whistle just blew at halftime, and we’re taking a moment to tip our caps to the opposition before the next bloodbath begins. It’s just another reminder that The Duskbloods is a fun, friendly competition first and foremost, even if our surroundings are dismal and bleak.

articles.title: Doom Composer Mick Gordon Contributes New Track to Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2
articles.summary: Auroch Digital and Big Fan Games have confirmed award-winning composer Mick Gordon has contributed a new track to its upcoming ’90s-inspired boomer shooter Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2.
articles.body:
Auroch Digital and Big Fan Games have confirmed award-winning composer Mick Gordon has contributed a new track to its upcoming ’90s-inspired boomer shooter Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2.

The first taste of the original track can be heard behind today’s new release date trailer for Boltgun 2, which is blasting its way onto PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S on October 14. It was additionally confirmed Boltgun 2 will also be coming to Switch 2 “shortly after” its debut on other platforms. The trailer showcases the first footage of the game’s chief antagonist, Vashtorr the Arkifane – described as the “daemonic demigod of inventors, engineers, scientists, and artisans.”

IGN’s latest preview of Boltgun 2 found it “brings the grimy, oppressive reality of the 42nd Millennium to life with a readable, pixelated style that evokes the essence of it in a way that even the most hyperrealistic renditions like Space Marine 2 struggle to match”, and that it “feels like undiluted 40K.”

Mick Gordon’s soundtracks for both 2016’s Doom and Doom Eternal are the stuff of legend, although they ultimately culminated in a very public feud involving Gordon and Doom Eternal executive producer Marty Stratton .

Despite this, however, it was announced earlier this month that Gordon will be performing the Doom 2016 soundtrack live at UK-based tech-metal and prog music festival RADAR 2027. While Gordon performed a medley of Doom tracks at The Game Awards 2016, RADAR 2027 will otherwise mark the first time the soundtrack has been performed in a live environment like this.

articles.title: Xbox Is Handling the Transition From Physical Media to Digital Much Better Than PlayStation Is
articles.summary: Xbox just announced its plan to let players digitize their physical games for use across any number of supported devices, from PCs to handhelds to (presumably) the upcoming Project Helix next-gen PC/console hybrid. And just like that, they've made PlayStation look even worse for its tone-deaf, player-last decision to stop selling physical copies of its games starting in early 2028.
articles.body:
Xbox just announced its plan to let players digitize their physical games for use across any number of supported devices, from PCs to handhelds to (presumably) the upcoming Project Helix next-gen PC/console hybrid. And just like that, they've made PlayStation look even worse for its tone-deaf, player-last decision to stop selling physical copies of its games starting in early 2028 — the backlash from which isn't going away .

Setting aside how rare it's been for Xbox to one-up PlayStation since the infamous "How to share your games on PS4" fatality move that killed the Xbox One before that generation even started, what matters in the end is that the digital future is happening, and Microsoft is handling that transition far, far better than Sony is.

And yes, it is a transition. If it's not, it's because it already happened . But this is where Xbox is respecting players and PlayStation isn't. While Sony cuts off physical media support entirely, Microsoft — who, by the way, has yet to officially say, "Yes we're still going to continue to sell games on discs," because they in fact might not be doing that if Helix ends up omitting an optical drive, as I'd expect it probably will for cost reasons, if nothing else — is laying out a clear plan for players that says, "Hey, we respect the game-purchasing choices you've made in the past, and we want you to be able to continue to have access to those in the future." And most importantly, "Here's how we're going to do it."

That last bit is the most significant part. I've spent years complaining about how Microsoft should message from a position of confidence and strength, rather than take the reactive, stepping-on-rakes defensive position that we've become accustomed to seeing from them. This disc-to-digital initative is the kind of thing that Xbox needs to do a heck of a lot more of. The company has picked a great time to be proactive, as physical media is proving to be a hot-button issue for gamers: as it should be, frankly. Game preservation matters. Having choices matters. We still need actual legislation from governments around the world to make sure that when a player buys something digitally, they actually own it and companies can't just revoke those purchases whenever the heck they feel like it, but that's a different conversation.

And so, Xbox will let players simply insert their discs into their Xbox console. and that ownership license converts into a digital copy of the game. "Your physical game library is more than a collection of discs," Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said . "It holds years of memories and stories worth preserving. Starting next week, Xbox Insiders can unlock a digital entitlement for supported physical games. We’ll start with thousands of titles and add more as we can."

There is no doubt a ton of work on the back end to make this a seamless experience for players, so I don't want to pretend that this was just some quick, "well duh!" kind of fix. Credit to the teams at Xbox who are working on this to bring it into reality. It's the same kind of effort that went into Xbox's player-first backwards compatibility initiative. From a gamer's perspective, this is exactly how it should be. Respect our game discs, let them continue to work, but provide players an easy way to bring those games forward into the next generation of Xbox hardware as physical media, by and large, recedes into the hedges like that Homer Simpson gif.

It remains to be seen whether Xbox's disc-to-digital program will eventually extend all the way back to Xbox 360 and, dare I hope, original Xbox games. The good news here is that Xbox's history with this kind of initiative suggests that there's a good chance they will. But for right here and now, Xbox is doing the right thing here and doing it the right way: respect your players, and perhaps in time, that will translate to some new (or regained) loyalty. Kudos to Microsoft here; they got this one right.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Avengers: Endgame Encore Will Include Two Sneak Peeks at Doomsday, But There's a Catch
articles.summary: Two sneak peeks at Avengers: Doomsday are coming to screenings of Avengers: Endgame Encore, though one of them will only be included in certain showings.
articles.body:
Two sneak peeks at Avengers: Doomsday are coming to screenings of Avengers: Endgame Encore, though one of them will only be included in certain showings.

As per an August 25 press release from Disney UK, Avengers: Endgame Encore will include an “exclusive look” at Avengers: Doomsday . It’s expected that this will at least partially account for the four extra minutes that have been added to the film’s total runtime, which fans noticed when AMC began listing showtimes late last week.

In bigger news, an “additional sneak peek” of the upcoming flick will also be included at showings on IMAX and Infinity Vision-certified screens. Thus far, it’s unclear how much time this will add to those screenings, and it’s possible that this glimpse at Doomsday could be part of the pre-show previews and not the actual film itself. Either way, fans are split as to whether or not sitting through a three hour-long movie they’ve already seen is actually worth it.

Avengers director Joe Russo has said it’s “critically important” that Marvel Studios re-release the film in theaters, calling it an "opportunity to create a bridge from Endgame to Doomsday in a very unique way.”

"You don’t always get the chance to re-release because it costs money, so the fact that we can enhance the story of Doomsday by bridging it to Endgame and these characters that we worked with for years that we love so much, and continue their story: It’s a really unique opportunity,” he said.

As told by Russo, Avengers Endgame: Encore will contain “footage that is set in the Doomsday story” that has been added to Endgame. It’s unclear as yet what this footage will be, exactly, but launching DLC for a seven-year-old film is rubbing some Marvel fans the wrong way.

D23 First Look Avengers: Doomsday Costumes and Props

According to one fan on Reddit, "It's literally four extra minutes of footage that will be in a YouTube short within two days," while another argued that it’s not worth the trouble of “getting a babysitter” and “spending $30-$40 for four minutes of footage.”

Avengers: Doomsday is shaping up to be a similarly-debated film; Robert Downey Jr.’s role as Victor Von Doom has left some fans convinced that Marvel is holding an ace up its sleeve, with theories abounding that, perhaps, the actor so iconic for playing Iron Man is merely an illusion or a different version of the character in an alternate reality.

Still others have noticed apparent changes in Dr. Doom’s eye color in different shots within Doomsday trailers, suggesting that these theories could hold some merit. For now, Marvel has been playing its cards close to the chest as the Doomsday clock ticks down to December 18, 2026.

articles.title: Ridley Scott Is Developing an Alien: Covenant Sequel With Michael Fassbender
articles.summary: Ridley Scott has confirmed he isn't done with the Alien franchise as he's developing a sequel to Alien: Covenant.
articles.body:
Ridley Scott has confirmed he isn't done with the Alien franchise, as he's developing a sequel to Alien: Covenant .

When speaking with the LA Times , Scott confirmed he is still developing a sequel to Alien: Covenant, one that would follow Michael Fassbender's character, David. Scott revealed that the film would see David creating a “brave new world for himself" and deal with AI going awry. The android character was introduced in Scott's Alien prequel, Prometheus, and returned for Alien: Covenant. Throughout the two films, it has become extremely clear that his character plays a significant role in the Alien universe.

The end of Covenant teased that his story was far from over, but that follow-up film has been in development hell for nearly a decade . Covenant itself missed the mark financially, and then Fox was acquired by Disney, which likely caused all kinds of issues with the film's development. Still, the Alien IP is very active with FX's Alien: Earth series and 2024's Alien: Romulus, which was a big hit. There's also the highly-anticipated Alien: Isolation 2 on the horizon for gamers.

Ridley Scott had previously stated that he wanted to make a whole series of Alien prequels that lead into the original film, and his follow-up to Covenant would be one of many entries to build up to that. As of right now, it's unclear when Ridley Scott plans to break out the chestbursters again. He just released The Dog Stars, starring Jacob Elordi ( which IGN gave a 5 ), and has a Treasure Planet adaptation with Hugh Jackman set to begin filming in November, a Bee Gees project at Paramount, and a variety of original films in different stages of development.

Scott is a prolific director who cranks out a movie every other year at this point, but he's also 88. He doesn't have any plans to stop making movies, but it'll be interesting to see if he can get to the next Alien movie within the next couple of years. A sequel to Alien: Romulus is also in the works at Fox, but there's no word on when that will arrive either.

articles.title: Chris Hansen Buys Advertisements for His True Crime Streaming Platform Before Every Single Screening of A24's Primetime Movie
articles.summary: Chris Hansen, best known as the host of Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator series, has purchased advertisements for his streaming platform that will play before every single screening of A24’s upcoming film adaptation of his rise to fame, Primetime.
articles.body:
Chris Hansen, best known as the host of Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator series, has purchased advertisements for his streaming platform that will play before every single screening of A24’s upcoming film adaptation of his rise to fame, Primetime.

The Hollywood Reporter received exclusive footage of the trailer, which reportedly shows the host walking into a kitchen before greeting viewers with a familiar line: “I’m going to need everyone in the theater to take a seat right over there.”

“Now, there are more platforms than ever before where this disturbing crime is being committed. Join us undercover every day on my streaming network, TruBlu,” he says as a QR code pops up on the screen.

TruBlu is a true crime-focused streaming network co-founded and co-owned by Hansen, which features undercover stings, investigative reporting, crime documentaries, and other such fare. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Hansen’s original plan for his TruBlu advertisement included a line calling A24’s Primetime movie a “Hollywood fantasy version” of real events — but due to fears of backlash from arthouse studio, it was cut from the final version.

It’s safe to say that Hansen isn’t too keen on Primetime. The host notably turned down a preliminary screening of the film, as told by the man himself during an interview with Fox News where he accused A24 of asking him to sign a “very restrictive agreement” before he could sit down in the theater.

“The lawyers at A24 wanted me to sign away my rights to my name, image, and brand, essentially, as well as any potential legal rights that would come out of the movie,” he stated. “I couldn’t sign that, so they didn’t show me the film. I went all the way over there. … But who’s going to sign something like that?

“If you look at the trailer, obviously it’s a very dramatized version. They had told me that it’s fictionalized in many aspects. I know other people have seen it who didn’t sign an NDA, and yet they wanted me to sign it.”

This claim was refuted by sources close to the situation, who told The Hollywood Reporter that Hansen was merely asked to sign a standard NDA to “prevent spoilers and protect the studio’s IP.”

Primetime , starring Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen, was partially inspired by a 2007 Esquire article penned by Luke Dittrich that focused on Texas District Attorney Bill Conradt, who committed suicide after becoming the target of one of Hansen’s predator stings. Primetime releases in theaters on September 25, 2026.

articles.title: 'I Think That Was a Big Flaw' — Uncharted 3 Designer Says the Game Was Hindered by Too Many Set Pieces
articles.summary: An ex-Naughty Dog designer believes that Uncharted 2's success may have negatively impacted the way Uncharted 3 was developed.
articles.body:
An ex-Naughty Dog designer believes that Uncharted 2's success may have negatively impacted the way Uncharted 3 was developed.

When speaking with FRVR , ex-Naughty Dog designer Benson Russell revealed that Uncharted 2's over-the-top setpieces may have negatively impacted Uncharted 3. He noted that the big set pieces, such as the train sequence, all came organically when producing the game, but that wasn't the case for Uncharted 3. Instead, the team came up with 10 or 12 set pieces, such as the cargo plane sequence, and came up with a plan to decide on a small handful that would actually make it into the game at a later date.

Unfortunately, that never happened, and almost all of them made it into the final product. As a result, writer and director Amy Hennig was forced into a situation where she had to write all of these big set pieces into the game because the designers had already started working on them.

Uncharted Games in (Chronological) Order

“It also kind of corners Amy [Hennig] a bit, right?” he said. “Because it’s like, ‘Oh, these are the set pieces we want to do’, and she’s like, ‘Well, now I have to find a way to shoehorn the ship in, so I guess we’ll have pirates and they’ll have a pirate leader.'"

Russell went on to say that he believes making the game in this way was "a big flaw." Uncharted 3 sold exceptionally well and was highly reviewed, even scoring a 10/10 from IGN at the time . However, it does rank lower on the list when compared to other games in the series. The cargo plane sequence, however, is a standout moment that even made its way into the Uncharted live-action film a decade later.

Naughty Dog concluded the Uncharted series back in 2016, but there are rumors that the studio is returning for Uncharted 5 soon . Although its only announced title is Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, Naughty Dog has confirmed that it has multiple projects in the works. As for when we'll start to see those other games, it's hard to say, but it wouldn't be surprising if they follow Intergalatic in a relatively rapid succession.

articles.title: Silent Hill Producer Says Konami Wants to Release a New Game in the Series Every Year
articles.summary: Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto says that Konami is gunning for annual releases of new games in its flagship horror franchise.
articles.body:
Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto says that Konami is gunning for annual releases of new games in its flagship horror franchise.

Okamoto divulged this news in an interview with Gamesradar at Gamescom 2026, explaining that Konami is looking for fresh takes on the well-trodden beats of the Silent Hill series to keep it from stagnating.

"Our aim is to, hopefully, have an annual release of new games," he told the outlet. “If we stay laser-focused on the same American setting, that would exhaust [narrative] possibilities, and also potentially cause fatigue for the playerbase."

Okamoto also confirmed that several unannounced Silent Hill projects are currently in development. "There are still many projects that are still [in] the works and very unannounced titles. So obviously, we can't go into specifics. But there are still many projects that we are currently exploring and working on as we speak,” he said.

"We would like to let players know that we have more experiences coming up, and many types of games that, we believe, will be able to provide positive kinds of surprises for players waiting for this for the series."

This information holds up with statements made by Konami’s president, Hideki Hayakawa, who said the company is actively invested in “rebooting” its most iconic IPs, specifically mentioning Silent Hill, Metal Gear , and Castlevania. (Though, in this case, the word 'reboot' seems to mean reinvigorating the franchises with new games, rather than remaking old ones.)

“Our company has been making games for more than 50 years, and we hold several IPs that are beloved globally by many fans. We concluded that rebooting these properties would be an effective way to make the most of them,” he said in an interview with Nikkei Gaming on July 23. “In addition to Metal Gear, Silent Hill, and Momotaro Dentetsu, we are also actively developing Castlevania (known in Japan as Akumajō Dracula).

“Our basic philosophy is that as long as there are customers for a given game, we will release it across multiple devices. Rather than focusing intensely on just one specific IP, we’ve built a structure that allows us to push forward on multiple IPs simultaneously with equal energy. That’s what this past year has looked like for us,” he explained.

Silent Hill has enjoyed a second wind with the Silent Hill 2 Remake and Silent Hill f, alongside the upcoming Silent Hill: Townfall , set to release on September 22. Silent Hill f , specifically, seems in line with Konami’s goals for the series, taking a drastic shift from its usual American setting in favor of 1960s Japan.

For more Silent Hill news, check out the official cast reveal trailer for Silent Hill Townfall and keep an eye out on our coverage from this year’s Gamescom .

articles.summary: Double Fine Productions, who recently regained the rights to its entire catalog following its pivot back to independence after Microsoft parted ways with several studios during its "Xbox reset," is honoring Tim Curry by making Brutal Legend free to download and own on PC for 666 minutes – until 3:06am PT/6:06am ET on Thursday, August 27.
articles.body:
Double Fine Productions, who recently regained the rights to its entire catalog following its pivot back to independence after Microsoft parted ways with several studios during its " Xbox reset ," is honoring Tim Curry by making Brutal Legend free to download and own on PC for 666 minutes – until 3:06am PT/6:06am ET on Thursday, August 27.

Curry, who passed away today at the age of 80, voiced Doviculus in Double Fine founder Tim Schafer's 2009 heavy metal strategy game Brutal Legend. "Rest in peace, dark prince," the company wrote on its itch.io page where you can download the game on PC. IGN's own Daemon Hatfield loved Brutal Legend, giving it a 9 out of 10 in his review . "Brutal Legend is a tour de force that wraps up humor, music, and clever gameplay into one highly polished package," Daemon wrote. "You haven't played a game quite like this before and won't want to miss it."

Curry was perhaps best known for his role in the cult classic film The Rocky Horror Picture Show, but also appeared in many video games besides Brutal Legend, including Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 (back in the FMV cutscene days!), Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers, and Dragon Age: Origins.

Double Fine, meanwhile, has announced that it is using its newfound independence to bring back its Amnesia Fortnight game jam as it looks to create its next project(s).
